questions.stem: The heart on the right shows a thickened ventricular wall with a smaller chamber cavity compared with the normal heart on the left. This geometry most directly predisposes to which functional type of heart failure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction

explanation.summary: A concentrically hypertrophied, stiff, small-cavity ventricle fills poorly during diastole while contractility is preserved, producing HFpEF (diastolic dysfunction).
explanation.whyCorrect: A concentrically hypertrophied, stiff, small-cavity ventricle fills poorly during diastole while contractility is preserved, producing HFpEF (diastolic dysfunction).

questions.stem: The point marked as ventricular dysfunction on this curve sits on the flattened, descending portion. For a dilated failing ventricle operating there, what happens to stroke volume when end-diastolic volume is increased further?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stroke volume rises in direct proportion to volume

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stroke volume rises little or actually falls

explanation.summary: On the descending/flattened limb of the Frank-Starling relationship, sarcomeres are already overstretched, so added volume yields little or no gain in stroke volume and can worsen output.
explanation.whyCorrect: On the descending/flattened limb of the Frank-Starling relationship, sarcomeres are already overstretched, so added volume yields little or no gain in stroke volume and can worsen output.
